# Introduction

PLACEHOLDER. The framing of the ACL submission carries over: the debate over
how much of a language model's output reflects learned linguistic
generalisation rather than reproduction of its training data, and binomials as
a test case with strong human baselines.

What changes is the evidence available. Section @sec-datasets describes an item
set roughly three times larger, screened for novelty against three corpora
rather than one, and a model set that spans six families and two orders of
magnitude of scale rather than four models from two families.

# Datasets {#sec-datasets}

## Novel binomials

We use `r N_ITEMS` novel binomials, each a plural Noun *and* Noun pair. An item
counts as novel only if the phrase itself is unattested: following the screen
in the ACL submission, we query four surface forms,

> *word1 and word2*, *Word1 and word2*, *word2 and word1*, *Word2 and word1*

and keep a pair only when all four return a count of zero.

Two things differ from the earlier version of this work. First, the screen runs
against the infini-gram index
(`api.infini-gram.io`)<!-- TODO: cite Liu et al. 2024, infini-gram. Pull the
official BibTeX from the ACL Anthology and add it to references.bib; it is the
one work cited here that the submission's custom.bib did not contain. -->
rather than a locally constructed n-gram corpus, which makes it reproducible
without redistributing a derived copy of the training data. Second, and more
importantly, **novelty is corpus-relative and we treat it as such.**

The earlier screen ran against Dolma alone, which is the training corpus for
the OLMo models but not for anything else. We therefore re-ran the identical
screen against every corpus for which an index exists and a model in our set
was trained on it:

| Corpus | Models trained on it | Novel |
|:--|:--|--:|
| Dolma v1.7 | OLMo ×3 | 458/458 |
| The Pile | Pythia ×7 | 444/458 |
| BabyLM | hand-trained ×3 | 458/458 |

: Novelty of the candidate item set by corpus. The Dolma figure independently
reproduces the original screen. {#tbl-novelty}

Fourteen candidate items are attested in the Pile, at counts of one or two in
300B tokens, so single incidental occurrences rather than conventionalised
phrases. They are **dropped for every model**, not only for the seven Pythia
models that saw them, so that the item set is identical across all
`r N_MODELS` models and the human participants. This costs 3.1% of items and
keeps every cross-model comparison on the same material.

GPT-2's WebText is not indexed, and the training corpora of Qwen3, Llama 3.2,
Gemma 3 and Mistral are not disclosed, so for those ten models novelty rests on
absence from Dolma, the Pile and BabyLM jointly rather than on their own
training data. We state this as a limitation rather than a guarantee.

## Abstract ordering preference

As in the ACL submission, each binomial carries a value for the ten constraints
of @morgan2015modeling, combined into a single abstract preference (AbsPref)
through their fitted logistic model. Positive values favour the alphabetically
first word, a neutral reference order. `Icon` is zero for every novel item here
and so contributes nothing and is dropped from any model that estimates
constraints individually.

Constraints enter the models on their **raw scales**. Each is a signed
difference whose zero means the two words are equal on that constraint, so
centring would move the origin off the one interpretable point and tie it to the
composition of this particular item set.

## Corpus bigram log-odds {#sec-bigram}

We control for corpus bigram statistics, to rule out surface co-occurrence as
the driver of model preferences. The phrase itself cannot serve: the trigram
*word1 and word2* has a count of zero for every item **by construction**, since
that is the novelty criterion. The control is therefore built from the component
bigrams, which are not zero.

This is the same quantity used in the earlier version of this work, where it was
written as a ratio of Markov-factored phrase probabilities. The unigram terms
and the shared count of *and* cancel between the two orderings, so that
expression reduces to the count form used here:

$$\log \frac{P(w_1\ \text{and}\ w_2)}{P(w_2\ \text{and}\ w_1)} = \log C(w_1\,\text{and}) + \log C(\text{and}\,w_2) - \log C(w_2\,\text{and}) - \log C(\text{and}\,w_1)$$ {#eq-bigram}

the unigram terms cancelling between the two orderings. Both transitions are
required to build the phrase, so the counts multiply rather than sum, and a zero
in either position collapses the estimate as it should. Counts carry a 0.5
pseudocount, which is load-bearing rather than cosmetic for the small corpus.

Because @eq-bigram is a contrast, multiplying every count by a constant cancels:
corpus **size** is irrelevant and corpus **composition** is not. The control is
therefore matched to each model's own training corpus where that corpus is
known: Pythia against the Pile, the hand-trained models against BabyLM, and
everything else against Dolma. That matching earns its keep. Dolma and the Pile
agree closely over these items ($r = .95$, 88% sign agreement), both being
scraped web text, while BabyLM, which is child-directed and transcribed speech,
agrees with them only at $r = .64$.

# Experiment 1: Novel Binomial Preferences

## Methods

### Language model predictions

We score `r N_MODELS` base models, listed in @tbl-models. Instruction-tuned
variants are excluded throughout: instruction tuning shifts sequence
probabilities in ways that would confound a comparison across scale.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-models
#| tbl-cap: "Models scored, by family and parameter count. All are base (non-instruct) checkpoints."

llm$coverage %>%
  transmute(Model = str_remove(as.character(model), "^.*/"),
            Family = model_family,
            `Params (M)` = params) %>%
  arrange(`Params (M)`) %>%
  kbl(booktabs = TRUE, longtable = TRUE) %>%
  kable_styling(latex_options = c("repeat_header"))
```

For each item, the preference is the difference in summed token
log-probability between the two orderings,

$$\texttt{preference} = \log P(\text{prompt} + w_1\ \text{and}\ w_2) - \log P(\text{prompt} + w_2\ \text{and}\ w_1)$$ {#eq-pref}

computed in each of `r N_PROMPTS` prompt contexts. The prompt is identical in
both strings and so cancels in the difference. Sequence log-probabilities are
not length normalised, for consistency with @houghton2025role.

### Analyses

For each model we fit two specifications, each in two arms. The first
specification takes abstract preference as the predictor; the second takes the
nine constraints that vary across these items, entered simultaneously. Each is
fit once as stated and once with the corpus bigram log-odds of @sec-bigram
added, giving four analyses per model.

All are Bayesian mixed-effects models fit in **brms** [@burkner2017brms] with
weak priors, four chains of 4,000 iterations, and sum contrasts.

$$\texttt{preference} \sim \texttt{AbsPref} + (\texttt{AbsPref} \mid \text{prompt}) + (1 \mid \text{Item})$$ {#eq-m1}

$$\texttt{preference} \sim \texttt{AbsPref} + \texttt{BigramLogOdds} + (\texttt{AbsPref} \mid \text{prompt}) + (1 \mid \text{Item})$$ {#eq-m2}

$$\texttt{preference} \sim \sum_{k} \texttt{Constraint}_k + (1 \mid \text{prompt}) + (1 \mid \text{Item})$$ {#eq-m3}

$$\texttt{preference} \sim \sum_{k} \texttt{Constraint}_k + \texttt{BigramLogOdds} + (1 \mid \text{prompt}) + (1 \mid \text{Item})$$ {#eq-m4}

Two departures from the ACL submission are worth stating. First, the bigram
control enters **additively** rather than as an interaction with AbsPref. The
question the control exists to answer is whether abstract preference survives
once surface statistics are in the model, which is what an additive term tests;
an interaction asks the different question of whether the AbsPref effect varies
with bigram probability, and spends a parameter on it. Second, we retain all
nine varying constraints rather than dropping those with the highest variance
inflation. Collinearity among constraints inflates intervals but does not bias
the estimates, and dropping constraints changes what the remaining coefficients
mean.

# Experiment 2: Human Judgments

## Methods

### Procedure

Participants complete a two-alternative forced choice task, choosing the
ordering that sounds more natural. Items and the two options are both presented
in randomised order.

One procedural change from the ACL submission is material to the analysis. In
that version the alphabetical ordering was **always displayed on the left**, so
any left/right response bias was confounded with the alphabetical contrast and
could not be estimated. The current build assigns the side in balanced pairs:
each successive pair of trials places the alphabetical option on each side once,
in random order, so the split is exactly even over any even number of trials and
off by one over an odd number. The side shown is recorded per trial, which makes
side bias an estimable nuisance effect rather than an unmeasured confound.

### Analyses

As in Experiment 1, abstract preference and the individual constraints are each
fit with and without the bigram control. The outcome is the binary choice.

Two nuisance predictors ride along in every model: position in the run, and
which side the alphabetical ordering was shown on. Both enter as fixed effects
with by-participant random slopes. Left and right are the complete set of sides
rather than a sample from a population of sides, which is what makes side a
fixed effect; the by-participant slope is the random part, and is the quantity
of interest in any case, since it asks whether individual people carry a side
bias.

Random effects are maximal in the sense of @barr2013random, subject to the
constraint that a predictor can take a random slope only for a grouping factor
within which it varies. The constraints are item properties and so are constant
within item: they can take by-participant slopes but not by-item ones. Side and
trial position vary within both and take slopes for both.

$$\texttt{chose alphabetical} \sim \texttt{AbsPref} + \texttt{trial} + \texttt{side} + (\texttt{AbsPref} + \texttt{trial} + \texttt{side} \mid \text{Participant}) + (\texttt{trial} + \texttt{side} \mid \text{Item})$$ {#eq-h1}

# Limitations

PLACEHOLDER. Carries over from the ACL submission, plus two additions: novelty
